full_judgment:
7. After the closure of the evidence, the accused-appellant was examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to which he again pleaded his innocence and desire to submit a written statement and the learned Special Sessions Judge accepted the same. 

 10. Ms. Rimi Nahreen, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the accused-appellant taking me through the impugned judgment, evidence, and other materials on record at the very outset contends that as the prosecution has failed to establish its case on point of identification of the accused in the TI parade the learned Special Sessions Judge ought to have acquitted the accused-appellant of the charge leveled against him. She then contends that the informant who was examined as PW 2 admitted that he saw the appellant before the TIP; PW 3 in his chief did not mention identify the appellant at the TI Parade, rather the learned Special Sessions Judge without considering the same most illegally convicted the appellant. She lastly contends that recognition of the appellant in the TI parade is a weak type of evidence which if not supported by other evidence cannot form the basis of conviction. In support of her contention, she has cited several decisions namely, Ibrahim and others vs The State as reported in 10 MLR (HCD) 62, Abdul Mannan vs The State as reported in 17 BLD (HCD) 290 = 1 BLC 195. 

 11. Ms Anwara Shahjahan learned Deputy Attorney-General for the state opposes the contention so made by the learned counsel for the accused-appellant and contends that the learned Special Sessions Judge rightly considered that PW-2 and PW-3 identified the accused-appellant in the TI parade. So, the learned trial court by considering the evidence on record rightly convicting the accused-appellant. 

 12. Be that as it may, to substantiate the submission se made by the learned counsels and proper adjudication of the matter. I have gone through the impugned judgment, the evidence, and other materials on record. It appears that the prosecution side to proved its case examined as many as 5(five) witnesses out of 6(six) charge-sheeted witnesses. Of them, PW-1 sub-inspector Murad Hossain deposed that he was the officer in charge of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court-Hajatkhana at that time. He then stated that accused-appellant Moinul Haque was put up along with other accused of the same age for the TI parade. The TI parade was held in presence of the learned Magistrate Munshi Abdul Mazid. The accused-appellant was identified by the informant and another witness of the case, he signed on the TI parade report as a witness. 

 13. PW 2 Md Joynal Abedin, the informant of the instant case deposed that on 27-11-2009 at about 5-30 pm he along with his assistant Md Asad was on a rickshaw on the way to Dhanmondi Hawkers Market and they had Taka 3,60,000. He then asserted in his evidence that while they were passing the bachelor stuff quarter 4(four) unknown persons with 2(two) motorcycle obstructed their way and forcefully taken them to inside the Padma oil under the Dhaka airport area. He then stated that he recognised the accused when he took off his helmet. He gave money to the accused. In the cross-examination, he admitted that he did not state in the FIR that he recognised the accused when he took off his helmet. He then admitted that he saw the accused-appellant at the Paltan police station before the TI parade. 

 14. PW 3 Md Asad stated in his evidence that on 27-12-2010 afternoon at about 5-30 pm he along with Joynal Abedin by rickshaw on the way to Dhanmondi Hawkers Market and while they were passing the bachelor staff-quarter 4(four) unknown persons came forward and stoped their rickshaw; they introduced themselves as police personnel and forcefully taken them to their motorcycles and rushed to the bush of the Padma oil beside the airport. He then stated that they stanched Taka 3,60,000 and 2(two) mobile sets from them. 

 16. PW 5 Police Inspector Md Jasim Uddin, the investigating officer of the instant case. He stated in his evidence that the instant case was investigated by him and after investigation, he submitted the charge-sheet against the accused-appellant. 

 17. These are all evidence available on the record. 

 20. It is important to note that in the instant case PW 2 the identifying witness, admitted in the cross-examination that he saw the accused-appellant in the Paltan police station before the TI Parade. Moreover, this witness asserted in his deposition that he recognised the accused-appellant when he took off his helmet, rather in the cross-examination he admitted that he did not state in the First Information Report that the accused-appellant was recognised by him when he took off his helmet. From the above, it appears that the PW 2 got an opportunity to see the accused-appellant before the TI Parade. On the contrary, PW3 another identifying witness who had not been asked in his examination-in-chief about identifying the accused-appellant at the TI parade. Had he been asked it would have gone against the prosecution. Moreover, PW 1 and PW 4 (Magistrate) did not mention in their evidence that the appellant was identified in the TI Parade by the PW 3. Basing on this principle as stated in section 114g of the Evidence act this omission of the prosecution benefits the accused-appellant. As such it would be unsafe to convict the accused-appellant on such identification evidence unless corroborated by some other evidence. 

 21. From Exhibit-2 it appears that the photocopy of the memorandum of TIP was exhibited which was lost its credibility as the prosecution failed to produce the original memorandum of TIP to prove that it was not without the signature of the conducting magistrate and no explanation as to why the original memorandum was not produced. Thus this photocopy of the memorandum of TIP is not admissible in evidence as per proviso so enumerated in section 65 of the Evidence Act. 

 22. Nevertheless, it is now well settled that circumstantial evidence must be so strong as to eliminate the possibility of the innocence of the accused. In other words, the circumstantial evidence must not be incompatible with the innocence of the accused. In the instant, it appears from the record that there is no direct evidence or circumstantial which is incompatible with the innocence of the accused-appellant.
